Author: Mary Astell (1666–1731)
About: English philosopher and early feminist writer from Newcastle. Her Serious Proposal to the Ladies argued for a women's academic retreat, and Some Reflections upon Marriage critiqued the subordination of wives. She corresponded with John Norris on the love of God and was a High Church Tory polemicist.

Author: James Balfour of Pilrig (1705–1795)
About: Scottish advocate and later Professor of Moral Philosophy and then of Public Law at Edinburgh. His Delineation of the Nature and Obligation of Morality (1753) defended a rationalist, religiously grounded morality against Hume's sentimentalism.

Author: George Berkeley (1685–1753)
About: Irish philosopher, educated at Trinity College Dublin, and later Bishop of Cloyne. Best known for immaterialism ('to be is to be perceived') in the Principles and Three Dialogues; also wrote on vision, mathematics (The Analyst) and tar-water (Siris).

Author: Elizabeth Burnet (1661–1709)
About: English religious writer and philanthropist, third wife of Bishop Gilbert Burnet. Author of A Method of Devotion (1708), she corresponded with John Locke on philosophy and theology, notably on Shaftesbury and moral questions.

Author: Joseph Butler (1692–1752)
About: English Anglican bishop (Bristol, then Durham) and moral philosopher. His Fifteen Sermons (1726) offered an influential account of conscience, self-love and benevolence, and The Analogy of Religion (1736) answered the deists.

Author: Archibald Campbell (1691–1756)
About: Scottish minister and Professor of Ecclesiastical History at St Andrews. His Enquiry into the Original of Moral Virtue (1733) attacked Mandeville and argued that self-love underlies virtue; he faced heresy charges in the Church of Scotland.

Author: Sarah Chapone (1699–1764)
About: English writer (née Kirkham), friend of Samuel Richardson and Mary Delany. Her Hardships of the English Laws in Relation to Wives (1735) is a pointed critique of coverture and the legal powerlessness of married women.

Author: Lady Mary Chudleigh (1656–1710)
About: English poet and essayist from Devon. The Ladies Defence (1701) was a verse dialogue rebutting a sermon on wifely obedience; her Poems and Essays upon Several Subjects advocate women's learning and Stoic self-command.

Author: Samuel Clarke (1675–1729)
About: English Anglican clergyman and leading Newtonian philosopher. His Boyle Lectures gave a cosmological argument for God and a rationalist ethics of 'fitness'; he debated Dodwell and Collins on the soul and liberty, Leibniz on space and time, and was accused of Arianism over the Trinity.

Author: Catharine Trotter Cockburn (1679–1749)
About: English playwright, novelist and philosopher. After early success on the London stage (e.g. The Unhappy Penitent), she wrote a celebrated Defence of Locke's Essay and later works defending Clarke's moral rationalism; her Works were collected by Thomas Birch in 1751.

Author: Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688)
About: English theologian, Master of Christ's College and leading Cambridge Platonist. The True Intellectual System of the Universe (1678) attacked atheism and materialism; his posthumous Treatise concerning Eternal and Immutable Morality defended the objectivity of moral truths. Father of Damaris Masham.

Author: Judith Drake (fl. 1696–1723)
About: English writer and medical practitioner credited with An Essay in Defence of the Female Sex (1696), a witty argument that women's apparent inferiority stems from education, not nature. The essay was long attributed to Mary Astell.

Author: David Fordyce (1711–1751)
About: Scottish philosopher and Professor of Moral Philosophy at Marischal College, Aberdeen. His Elements of Moral Philosophy, influenced by Hutcheson, became a widely used textbook; he drowned in a shipwreck off the Dutch coast in 1751.

Author: Richard Gwinnett (d. 1717)
About: Gloucestershire gentleman and long-standing suitor of the poet Elizabeth Thomas, who died before they could marry. Their correspondence was published posthumously as The Honourable Lovers / Pylades and Corinna (1731–32).

Author: David Hume (1711–1776)
About: Scottish philosopher, historian and essayist, a central figure of the Scottish Enlightenment. His Treatise and Enquiries developed an empiricist account of causation, the passions and morality, and he was a sharp sceptic about religion in the Natural History of Religion and Dialogues.

Author: Francis Hutcheson (1694–1746)
About: Ulster-born philosopher and Professor of Moral Philosophy at Glasgow, often called the father of the Scottish Enlightenment. He developed the theory of a 'moral sense' and of benevolence against Hobbes and Mandeville, and taught Adam Smith.

Author: Thomas Johnson (d. 1737)
About: English cleric and Cambridge scholar (Magdalene College). His Essay on Moral Obligation (1731) intervened in the debate on whether moral duties rest on the will of God or on the nature of things, siding with a voluntarist view.

Author: Johnston (identity uncertain)
About: Author of The Eternal Obligation of Natural Religion (1732), a contribution to the rationalist debates sparked by Clarke and his critics. The author's full identity is not securely established; verify against the source edition before relying on this entry.

Author: William King (1650–1729)
About: Irish Anglican clergyman, Archbishop of Dublin. His De Origine Mali (1702) offered a theodicy explaining evil as compatible with a good God; it was translated with extensive notes by Edmund Law as An Essay on the Origin of Evil (1731).

Author: Edmund Law (1703–1787)
About: English cleric and philosopher, Master of Peterhouse and later Bishop of Carlisle. Translator of King's Origin of Evil; his Considerations on the Theory of Religion (1745) argued for progressive revelation, and he was associated with Lockean, latitudinarian theology.

Author: John Locke (1632–1704)
About: English philosopher and physician, founder of British empiricism. His Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Two Treatises of Government and Some Thoughts concerning Education were enormously influential; his voluminous correspondence includes Masham, Burnet and Cockburn.

Author: Bernard Mandeville (1670–1733)
About: Dutch-born physician and satirist who settled in London. The Fable of the Bees ('private vices, publick benefits') provoked fierce controversy by arguing that commercial prosperity rests on self-interest and vice; he also wrote on hypochondria and on honour.

Author: Damaris Cudworth Masham (1659–1708)
About: English philosopher, daughter of Ralph Cudworth and close friend of John Locke, who lived at her house at Oates. Her Discourse concerning the Love of God (1696) answered Norris and Astell, and Occasional Thoughts (1705) argued for women's education; she corresponded with Leibniz.

Author: Susanna Newcome (1685–1763)
About: English theological writer, wife of John Newcome, Master of St John's College, Cambridge. Her anonymously published Enquiry into the Evidence of the Christian Religion (1728) defended Christianity on rational grounds; the sacrament pieces in the corpus relate to the controversy over Hoadly's Plain Account.

Author: John Norris (1657–1711)
About: English clergyman and philosopher, rector of Bemerton, the leading English follower of Malebranche. He wrote on divine love, the ideal world and happiness, corresponded with Mary Astell, and criticised Locke.

Author: Alexander Pope (1688–1744)
About: English poet and satirist, the leading poet of the Augustan age. His philosophical poem An Essay on Man (1733–34), influenced by Bolingbroke, sought to 'vindicate the ways of God to man' and was defended by Warburton against charges of fatalism.

Author: Thomas Rutherforth (1712–1771)
About: English cleric and Regius Professor of Divinity at Cambridge. His Essay on the Nature and Obligations of Virtue (1744) criticised moral-sense theory in favour of a self-interested, theological basis for virtue, and his Institutes of Natural Law were lectures on Grotius.

Author: Anthony Ashley Cooper, 3rd Earl of Shaftesbury (1671–1713)
About: English philosopher and moralist, tutored as a child by Locke. His Characteristicks introduced the 'moral sense' and an aesthetic, benevolent ethics; Several Letters (1716) were addressed to a young student at Oxford.

Author: Adam Smith (1723–1790)
About: Scottish philosopher and economist, student of Hutcheson and friend of Hume. The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) grounded morality in sympathy and the 'impartial spectator'; he later wrote The Wealth of Nations (1776).

Author: Elizabeth Thomas (1675–1731)
About: English poet and letter-writer known as 'Corinna', a name given her by Dryden. Her Miscellany Poems (1722) include verse on women's education; she was satirised in Pope's Dunciad after selling his letters to Curll.

Author: George Turnbull (1698–1748)
About: Scottish philosopher and regent at Marischal College, Aberdeen, where he taught Thomas Reid. His Principles of Moral Philosophy (1740) applied Newtonian experimental method to ethics in a Shaftesburian, providentialist spirit.

Author: William Warburton (1698–1779)
About: English critic and controversialist, later Bishop of Gloucester. The Divine Legation of Moses argued that the absence of a future state in Mosaic law proved its divine origin; he defended Pope's Essay on Man and became Pope's literary executor.

Author: Isaac Watts (1674–1748)
About: English Nonconformist minister, theologian and celebrated hymn-writer. His Logick (1724) and The Improvement of the Mind were standard educational texts for over a century, broadly Lockean in outlook.
